query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated free-energy framework that combines CALPHAD thermodynamic databases, ab initio calculations, and high-fidelity sampling—calibrated with in situ DSC and synchrotron measurements—can accurately and efficiently predict the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys with errors below 10% across their broad compositional space.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in their solid-state configuration prior to melting.
generation.intervention: Apply a new sampling/free-energy modeling approach by integrating CALPHAD data with ab initio predictions and high-fidelity free-energy sampling. This approach is then calibrated and validated using high-temperature experimental techniques such as differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and synchrotron-based measurements at key compositions.
generation.conditions: Near-melting and melting conditions for a representative set of high-entropy alloys covering a wide compositional range.
generation.structural_mediator: The interplay of mixing enthalpies, vibrational entropy, and diffusion kinetics that govern phase stability and the solid-liquid transition in high-entropy alloys.
generation.mechanism: The combined framework is designed to capture both configurational and vibrational contributions to the free-energy landscape. By using CALPHAD for multicomponent phase diagram prediction and refining these predictions with ab initio and high-fidelity sampling methods—supported by targeted high-temperature experiments—the approach can more precisely resolve the thermodynamic parameters across complex alloy compositions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will yield predictions for melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting that agree with experimental measurements within an approximate 10% margin of error, significantly improving over current high-throughput screening methods that primarily focus on melting point estimations.
generation.baseline: Existing high-throughput computational methods that identify candidate high-entropy alloys mainly by estimated melting points without fully capturing fusion thermodynamics or volume changes.
generation.boundary: The approach’s accuracy may be limited in compositions where unexpected inter-element interactions or complex diffusion dynamics dominate, or if the assumptions in the ab initio models do not fully capture high-temperature vibrational effects.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the scalability of the ab initio component across the full HEA compositional space and whether vibrational and kinetic contributions at melting can always be captured within the targeted 10% error. Further, systematic deviations in certain composition regimes could indicate unaccounted phenomena.

falsification_experiment.design: Select multiple HEA compositions spanning the broad compositional range. For each, use in situ DSC and synchrotron X-ray measurements to determine key melting properties (melting temperature, enthalpy & entropy of fusion, volume change at melting). Compare these experimental results with the model predictions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If two or more compositions show deviations greater than 10% between the experimental measurements and the predicted values in any of the measured properties, then the proposed integrated free-energy framework is falsified for accurate description of HEA melting thermodynamics.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system. decision.trend: A high-throughput computational screening approach has been demonstrated for high-entropy alloys, exemplified by the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system in PMC8282813. They used theoretical methods to estimate melting points, filter large compositional spaces, and identify candidate alloys with high Tm. While this demonstrated the feasibility of computational discovery, it did not provide a fully validated methodology to precisely capture enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume changes at melting, or other liquid-phase thermodynamics for arbitrary HEA compositions.
decision.unsolved: Broadly mapping thermophysical properties over all composition space remains unachieved. It is unclear how to upscale current computational or experimental methods to accurately handle the range of compositional complexity without excessive cost. A potential decisive validation for any proposed approach would be a measured mismatch in melting temperature or fusion-related thermodynamics that significantly exceeds the claimed accuracy (e.g., >10% error for multiple carefully characterized HEAs), indicating that the underlying assumptions or computational frameworks are inadequate for certain HEA regimes.
decision.lever: Employ an advanced free-energy modeling framework (e.g., an integrated CALPHAD + ab initio + high-fidelity sampling approach) that systematically calculates thermodynamic functions across multi-component HEAs, validated at key compositions by in situ differential scanning calorimetry and synchrotron-based measurements. Critical parameters include mixing enthalpies, vibrational entropy, diffusion coefficients, and partial molar volumes.
decision.why: High-throughput computational filtering has shown promise in identifying plausible HEA compositions, but extending it to obtain robust, efficient predictions of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume changes at melting across the entire family requires a more comprehensive free-energy-based framework. By coupling ab initio models with data assimilation from targeted high-temperature experiments, this approach can reconcile theory with experimental reality and enable rigorous, predictive thermodynamic property determination.
